Supporting Participants: Payments, Benefits, and Indirect Costs

Hello Morgan State University Faculty & Staff, In this module, we will review key post-award processes for Participant Support Costs at Morgan State University. Topics include processing stipend requests, funding travel for research participants, processing tuition and fee remission, and understanding how participant support costs relate to indirect costs. Please note that the processes detailed in this module are specific to grant-funded activities. Some of the information may also be relevant to state-funded actions; however, policy and procedural differences may apply. We strive to continuously review these lessons to provide up-to-date guidance on Morgan’s sponsored project processes. For questions related to the activities covered in this module that are not addressed in the module content, please contact the ORA Training and Communications Coordinator: Mr. Ryan Mobley, CRA, CFRA, CPRA Email: ryan.mobley@morgan.edu Phone: 443-885-4771 Thank you, ORA Training Team

Self-paced ORA eTraining module. Source: https://share.articulate.com/fLyvCDI1vSeMFtSyq2ebF

What Are Participant Support Costs?
heading
ACCENT
Not every payment on a sponsored award is made for work performed or services rendered. In some cases, funds are provided to help an individual join, attend, or benefit from a training or educational experience connected to the award. These are known as participant support costs, and they may include expenses such as stipends, participant travel, registration fees, and other allowable costs that make participation possible. At Morgan State University, the key first step is determining whether the individual is truly a participant or trainee rather than an employee providing services to the project. Once that distinction is clear, the request can be reviewed and processed through the appropriate Morgan procedure with the documentation needed to support compliance.

Participant Cost Submission Tips
interactive
Review Notice of Award (NOA) for Restrictions
Are international students eligible to participate in this project? Are there sponsor-specific limits on stipend amounts, such as those that apply to NRSA -funded fellowships? Always review the project’s Notice of Award (NOA) to confirm that participant support costs align with the approved scope of work and are processed in accordance with sponsor requirements, Uniform Guidance, and Morgan State University policy.
Understand Impact in Banner
Participant support costs are typically budgeted to Pool 12 (Participant Support Costs) in Banner. However, certain participant-related expenses may post to other pool levels, such as non-MSU student stipends in Pool 02 (Contractual Salaries) and participant support travel in Pool 04 (Travel) . For awards with substantial participant support activity, it may be helpful to establish a separate project index dedicated to participant support funds. For assistance with this process, please contact the Restricted Funds Accounting (RFA) team at rfa@morgan.edu .
Indirect Costs (IDC) & Budget Transfers
Budget transfers out of the participant support cost pool are generally unallowable without prior written sponsor approval . When submitting any transfer request involving participant support costs, it is critical to provide supporting documentation showing sponsor approval to both the Office of Research Administration ( ORA) Budget Officers and the RFA team . Participant support costs are excluded from the Modified Total Direct Cost (MTDC) base used to calculate indirect costs. Because of this, transferring funds into or out of participant support budgets may affect the project’s indirect cost calculations and should be reviewed carefully. For additional guidance on MTDC calculations, please refer to the Indirect Costs & MTDC lesson of this module.
Stipends are for Support, Not Employment
Stipend support should not be used as a substitute for an employment contract when an employment arrangement is the more appropriate mechanism. For additional guidance on the distinction between stipend support and employment contracts, please refer to the Stipend vs. Contract: Which is Appropriate? lesson of this module.

## Stipend Vs. Contract: Which is Appropriate?

text
Employee Contract vs. Participant Stipend
heading
ACCENT
interactive
Employee
Employment Contract An employment contract is used when the institution pays an employee for work on a sponsored project, such as salary, wages, or summer research contracts. The core idea is compensation for services rendered. Under Uniform Guidance ( 2 CFR 200.430 ), this is employee compensation and is tied to actual work benefiting the award. Hallmarks of a Contract There is a defined service, deliverable, or work expectation. Pay is tied to the work being performed. Documentation often includes scope of work or position description, dates, pay rate, deliverables, approvals, and payment terms. Employee pay usually carries payroll treatment and associated fringe benefit charges.
Participant
Stipend Support A stipend is not pay for services. It is subsistence support given to a participant, fellow, or trainee so they can take part in training or another eligible educational activity. Uniform Guidance includes stipends within participant support costs, and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) states directly that stipends support living expenses during training and are not employee compensation. The National Science Foundation (NSF) similarly describes participants as people whose primary purpose is learning or receiving training and who receive a stipend rather than salary and fringe benefits. Hallmarks of a Stipend The primary purpose is training or participation, not labor. The amount is often predetermined. It is not based on hours worked. It is not paid in exchange for institutional services like staffing a lab, entering data, coordinating recruitment, or managing project operations. It is only appropriate when the sponsor and the award purpose allow it. At institutes of higher education (IHEs), federal rules say scholarships, fellowships, and student aid are allowable only when the award’s purpose is to provide training to participants and the agency approves the cost.

Tuition Remission on Sponsored Projects
heading
ACCENT
When the Office of Research Administration receives a new Notice of Award, our team reviews the award carefully to determine whether tuition remission is included as part of the project budget. If it is, the next step falls to the ORA Budget Officers, who request a detail code from the Office of Financial Aid. In practice, a detail code acts like the institutional link that tells the system (Banner) where those charges belong. Without that detail code in place, tuition charges cannot be assigned to the project budget in Banner.

Participant Travel on Awards
heading
WHITE
ACCENT
image
Notes
Participant travel refers to travel costs provided for individuals under a sponsored project as trainees, attendees, or other supported participants, rather than as employees working on the award. In Banner, these costs are charged to the 04 (Travel) pool level, even though the travel is for participant support purposes. For awards with significant participant support costs, including travel, it may be helpful to establish a separate index to keep those expenses clearly separated from other project charges. The RFA team can assist with creating that index when needed. If a separate index is not created, it is important to work closely with your project's RFA accountant to ensure participant travel expenses are not inadvertently included in indirect cost calculations. From a processing standpoint, participant travel documents move through the same travel request (TL Form) and reimbursement process used for other travel-related expenses on Morgan awards. A clear process map for travel requests is included in the Travel on Sponsored Projects: From Approval to Reimbursement e-module.

rise/courses/U5tbyEz4mfS5hz3yGEKU7g759i4_LQ2z/g6MVNr3jCTk2LV0k.jpg
Modified Total Direct Costs, or MTDC , is the portion of a project budget that many institutions, including Morgan State, use as the base for calculating indirect costs. In simple terms, MTDC is not the full project budget. Instead, it includes certain direct cost categories while leaving out specific items that are excluded from the indirect cost calculation. At Morgan, this means indirect costs are not assessed on expenses excluded from MTDC, such as participant support costs, equipment, capital expenditures, and the portion of each subaward over $25,000 . When you look at the infographic below, think of MTDC as the “allowable base” on which the IDC rate is applied, rather than every dollar charged to the award. Current Morgan State indirect cost rates can be found on the ORA's F&A Cost Rates page.

Budget Transfers & MTDC
Budget transfers can affect indirect cost needs when funds move between MTDC and non-MTDC cost categories. Costs excluded from the MTDC base, such as participant support, equipment, capital expenditures, and the portion of each subaward over $25,000, do not generate indirect costs. As a result, moving funds from an MTDC category into one of these excluded categories can reduce the amount of indirect costs needed on the project and free up more funds for direct costs. The opposite is also true: moving funds from an excluded category into an MTDC cost category increases the MTDC base, which means additional funds may be needed to cover the associated indirect costs.
Knowledge check: A sponsored project has the following budgeted costs: Salaries and Wages: $80,000 Fringe Benefits: $20,000 Travel: $10,000 Equipment: $15,000 Participant Support Costs: $5,000 Subaward: $40,000 If the institution uses a MTDC base, what amount should be used to calculate indirect costs?
  - $150,000  [incorrect]
  - $135,000  [CORRECT ANSWER]
  - $140,000  [incorrect]
  - $110,000  [incorrect]
  If correct: Great job! MTDC includes salaries and wages, fringe benefits, travel, and only the first $25,000 of each subaward. It excludes equipment and participant support costs. So the calculation is: $80,000 + $20,000 + $10,000 + $25,000 = $125,000
  If incorrect: Try again!
  Note on "$150,000": Try Again!
  Note on "$135,000": Great job! MTDC includes salaries and wages, fringe benefits, travel, and only the first $25,000 of each subaward. It excludes equipment and participant support costs. So the calculation is: $80,000 + $20,000 + $10,000 + $25,000 = $135,000
  Note on "$140,000": Try Again!
  Note on "$110,000": Try Again!
Knowledge check: A grant has an indirect cost rate of 54% MTDC for on-campus research. A department transfers $10,000 from their Supplies budget line to their Equipment budget line. How does this transfer affect the project's indirect cost needs?
  - Indirect cost needs increase by $5,400  [incorrect]
  - Indirect cost needs decrease by $5,400  [CORRECT ANSWER]
  - Indirect cost needs do not change  [incorrect]
  - Direct cost needs decrease by $5,400  [incorrect]
  If correct: Great job! Supplies are typically included in the MTDC base, while equipment is excluded. Moving $10,000 out of Supplies and into Equipment reduces the MTDC base by $10,000. At an indirect cost rate of 54% the project would need $5,400 less budgeted for indirect costs.
  If incorrect: Try again!
  Note on "Indirect cost needs increase by $5,400": Try Again!
  Note on "Indirect cost needs decrease by $5,400": Great job! MTDC includes salaries and wages, fringe benefits, travel, and only the first $25,000 of each subaward. It excludes equipment and participant support costs. So the calculation is: $80,000 + $20,000 + $10,000 + $25,000 = $125,000
  Note on "Indirect cost needs do not change": Try Again!
  Note on "Direct cost needs decrease by $5,400": Try Again!
